title: Not from desire
hookLine: by the star, your companion is not astray, nor does he speak from desire (53:1–3)
carry: you know better the affairs of your world
tomorrow: The lote tree of the boundary

lines: NOTHING BUT TRUTH FROM THIS MOUTH.
cards: A young man named 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr used to write down everything the Prophet ﷺ said. Every word.
Some men of Quraysh told him to stop: he's a human being, they said, he speaks in anger and in good moods; why write it all? So 'Abdullah stopped, and went to ask.
The Prophet pointed to his own mouth and told him to keep writing. Nothing comes out of this, he said, except truth. Today's surah has a verse behind that answer.

teach.h: BY THE STAR AS IT SETS.
teach.b: Surah An-Najm, the Star, the fifty-third, opens with one oath. Pickthall's translation: "By the Star when it setteth, Your comrade erreth not, nor is deceived; Nor doth he speak of (his own) desire." Which star?
Commentators differ: the Pleiades, a falling star, any star at its setting. The oath is by something going down, out of sight, while what the surah defends stays.

Then: your comrade, sahibukum. Not the Prophet or the Messenger, but your companion, the man who grew up among you; the verse speaks to people who knew him. Then the key line: wa ma yantiqu 'anil-hawa.
Nor does he speak from desire.

Hawa is the desire that pulls you along, the word from the day desire was read as a god. Here the surah says the one bringing the message isn't driven by it. The next verse: it is nothing but revelation revealed.

teach.h: HOW FAR IT REACHES: SCHOLARS WEIGH IT.
teach.b: Scholars have discussed it carefully. It covers the Qur'an, first of all.
Sunni scholarship has long held that his teaching in religious matters, the Sunnah, also rests on revelation in a broader sense, one reason hadith became a source of law.
Scholars also point to a report where he gave an opinion in a worldly matter, how to pollinate date palms, and later said: you know better the affairs of your world.
On this reading, the verse isn't a claim that he never had a personal view. It's a claim about the message: it isn't self-serving, and it isn't his wanting dressed up as revelation.

how: Muslims cite 53:3–4 as a basis for following the Prophet's Sunnah alongside the Qur'an, and scholars of hadith built careful methods for recording and checking his words.

o: a sudden flash of divine inspiration
desire that pulls a person along
the air or wind blowing across sand

games.q: not from desire — tap the pairs.

s: scholars agree on which star 53:1 means
some say the Pleiades, some a falling star, some any star at its setting.
the verse calls the Prophet 'your companion'
sahibukum: the man they had known all his life.
the Prophet said every remark he made about farming was revelation
in the date-palm report he said: you know better the affairs of your world.

games.q: you're 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr. men of Quraysh tell you to stop writing the Prophet's words. what does he tell you?
o: keep writing; nothing but truth comes from this mouth.
write only what he says in a good mood.
games.why: he pointed to his mouth and told him to write, in a report in Sunan Abi Dawud.

practice: Think of a conversation coming up today: advice you'll give, a recommendation, an opinion at work.

Ask yourself honestly where your words might lean toward what you want, looking good, winning, getting your way, and choose one place to say what's true and useful for the other person, even if it gains you nothing.
If you pray, you can ask for an honest tongue.

wordCard.voice: Hawa: the desire that pulls a person along; 53:3 says the Prophet does not speak from it, only revelation. Today's word.
